2.2.3.1-f109.accuracy_reason: The Somnium (published posthumously in 1634) and the Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo (1610), Kepler's reply to Galileo, are both correctly identified.

2.2.3.1-f121.accuracy_reason: 'Apelles' was indeed Scheiner's pseudonym for his 1612 sunspot letters, and Burton's text does leave 'the Hollander' unnamed.

2.2.3.1-f122.accuracy_reason: In Icaromenippus 20–21 the Moon complains of the natural philosophers and asks Menippus to take a message to Zeus. 'Loosely echoes' is suitably hedged.

2.2.3.1-f125.accuracy_reason: The phrase belongs to the disclaimer Burton quotes from Cunaeus's Sardi venales (1612), and Burton does then pivot to 'not in jest, but in good earnest'.

2.2.3.1-f126.accuracy_reason: The words come from Minucius Felix, Octavius ch. 5, where the pagan Caecilius argues that the world is ruled by chance, not providence.

2.2.3.1-f136.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Epistles 2.1.244, on Alexander's poor judgment of poetry (he patronised Choerilus).

2.2.3.1-f208.accuracy_reason: The phrase is Tacitus, Histories 5.6, on Mount Lebanon, and the note correctly says that the marked word is only the author's name.

2.2.3.1-f229.accuracy_reason: Salt, sulphur and mercury are indeed the Paracelsian tria prima.

2.2.3.1-f230.accuracy_reason: Petrus Peregrinus's Epistola de magnete (1269) even describes a magnetic perpetual-motion wheel, and the note rightly says 'probably'.

2.2.3.1-f29.accuracy_reason: This is the standard definition of the limbus patrum.

2.2.3.1-f30.accuracy_reason: Revelation 14:20 in the Vulgate does read 'de lacu' and 'usque ad frenos equorum'. Burton's 200 Italian miles equals 1,600 stadia at 8 stadia to the mile.

2.2.3.1-f352.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Job 9:6 reads 'Qui commovet terram de loco suo, et columnae eius concutiuntur'. Burton's 'ver. 4' is wrong.

2.2.3.1-f360.accuracy_reason: Cunaeus's Sardi venales is a Menippean satire, and its disclaimer that nothing written is true plainly echoes the preface to Lucian's True History; the note says 'echoes', which is suitably cautious.

2.2.3.1-f46.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 5.6, has 'tantos inter ardores opacum fidumque nivibus' of Lebanon, so the omission and the change of subject are described correctly.

2.2.3.1-f6.accuracy_reason: Marco Polo (Burton's 'Polus') describes the rukh of Madagascar this way: feathers twelve paces long, and strong enough to lift an elephant.

2.2.3.1-f68.accuracy_reason: The Peripatetic quinta essentia is the aether, the incorruptible matter of the heavens.

2.2.3.1-f77.accuracy_reason: Andrea Corsali wrote to Giuliano de' Medici from Cochin in January 1516 (often dated 1516/17). The letter describes the cross and the two small clouds near the south pole, which are the Southern Cross and the Magellanic Clouds.

2.2.3.1-f79.accuracy_reason: 'Species' as emanated forms is right. Dee's Propaedeumata aphoristica (1558) is built on Bacon's theory of the multiplication of species, and Bacon wrote De multiplicatione specierum. The identification is suitably hedged.

2.2.3.1-f80.accuracy_reason: The question refers to the waters above the firmament in Genesis 1:7, and Burton's English does go on to discuss the question rather than translate it.

2.2.3.1-f87.accuracy_reason: The line is Aeneid 10.248. There it describes Aeneas's ship after the nymph pushes it on, and Burton applies it to the speed of the heavens.

2.2.3.1-f90.accuracy_reason: In astronomy, motion 'in longum' and 'in latum' means motion in longitude (along the ecliptic) and in latitude.
